> **Series**: *Bayesian Modelling for Industrial Applications*, Part 3. [Part 1](https://sambaiga.github.io/pages/blog/posts/2025/10/2025-10-10-bayesion-foundation.html) introduced Bayesian thinking, and [Part 2](https://sambaiga.github.io/pages/blog/posts/2025/12/2025-12-1-bayesian-regression..html) fitted one Beta regression to the six cells of one chemistry.

An operator of a battery fleet has to decide at every inspection whether to retire a cell or to leave it in service. A cell that has fallen below 80% of its nominal capacity is at the end of its useful life. The operator does not see the state of health directly, only diagnostics measured in the cycle, and a manufacturer that introduces a new chemistry has tested only a few cells of it. Part 2 gave the six cells of one chemistry the same degradation curve. That was a sensible first model, and its test showed the limit: predicted from the other five, four cells were followed closely and two were missed. Cells differ, and cells of one chemistry resemble each other more than they resemble cells of another, so the question is how far a new cell should be believed to resemble the cells that have been seen.

This post answers it with a hierarchical model, in which each cell draws its parameters from its chemistry and each chemistry from the whole fleet. The model is built with PyMC[^1] and fitted to the CALCE cycling data of Part 2, now with both chemistries. The post shows the priors before and after the data, checks how far the conclusions depend on the prior of the precision, and scores the model against its two obvious alternatives, one curve for all cells and one curve per cell, on the cells that it was fitted to. The hierarchy separates the two chemistries sharply. [The second post of Part 3](../../../../../pages/blog/posts/2026/11/2026-11-28-hierarchical-bayesian-retirement.llms.md) tests it on two cells that it never saw and turns its predictions into the retirement decision of the operator.

### Levels of Pooling

The question of how far a new cell resembles the cells already seen has three answers, which are called levels of pooling, and [Figure 1](#fig-pooling) draws them for the 13 cells of this study. Under **complete pooling** every cell shares one set of curve parameters, so a new cell receives the average curve of the fleet and its chemistry plays no part. Under **no pooling** each cell has parameters of its own and nothing is shared, so a cell is described by its own record only, and a cell without a record is described by the prior. **Partial pooling** lies between them: the parameters of a cell come from a distribution that belongs to its chemistry, and the parameters of a chemistry come from a distribution over the fleet. A cell with a long record is then free to move away from its chemistry, and a cell with a short or incomplete record is drawn towards it.

Show the code of the figure

``` python
for diagram in (concepts.complete, concepts.none, concepts.partial):
    show(diagram(CHEMISTRY_OF, HELD_OUT, COLOURS))
```

\(a\) Complete pooling

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

\(b\) No pooling

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

\(c\) Partial pooling

Figure 1: Three ways of tying the 13 cells together: one curve for the fleet, one curve for each cell, and a level for each chemistry between the fleet and its cells. Hollow rings mark the two held-out cells.

The three diagrams differ in what lies above the cells and so in what each strategy believes about a cell that it has not seen. The hollow rings are the two cells that are held out of the fits to test that belief, one of each chemistry. Complete pooling has no way to tell the new cells apart, no pooling has nothing to say about them except the prior, and partial pooling starts each of them from the level of its own chemistry. The choice matters most when records are short or incomplete, because the data then say little about a cell and the structure of the model decides what is believed. The sections that follow measure that on a real fleet, and the first of them describes the data.

### Thirteen Cells, Two Chemistries

The data are the cycle-by-cycle diagnostics of 13 lithium-ion cells from the CALCE laboratory, in the form prepared for Part 2.[^2] Six cells are of chemistry CS2, with a nominal capacity of 1.10 Ah, and seven are of chemistry CX2, with 1.35 Ah. Every cell was cycled until it fell well below the end-of-life threshold of 80% state of health (SoH). The target is the SoH, the capacity divided by the nominal capacity, divided again by 1.1 so that it stays inside the open unit interval that a Beta likelihood requires. SoH exceeds 100% in 1.7% of the cycles, which the ceiling of 1.1 accommodates. The inputs are the four diagnostics of Part 2, standardised on the training cells only.

Every eighth cycle is kept, because neighbouring cycles are almost duplicates, which leaves 1,752 observations with between 78 and 196 per cell. Two cells, CS2_38 and CX2_38, the last of each chemistry, are held out to test the strategies on cells that the model has not seen, and the remaining 11 cells provide 1,456 observations for training. The inputs are measured in the same cycle as the capacity, which is what an operator has at an inspection, so the model estimates the state of health from diagnostics and does not forecast it.

Show the code of the figure

``` python
show(lambda: hierarchy.curves(data, HELD_OUT, COLOURS))
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 2: State of health of the 13 cells against cycle. CX2 cells are orange and CS2 cells blue, dashed lines are the two cells held out for testing, and the dotted line is the end-of-life threshold of 80%.

The two chemistries differ markedly, as [Figure 2](#fig-curves) shows. The CX2 cells last up to 2,474 cycles and decline slowly, while the CS2 cells fail between 737 and 1,056 cycles. The records are not equally complete. CX2_16 begins at cycle 463 with a state of health of 94%, and CX2_33 begins at cycle 187, so for these two cells the early part of the curve is not observed. What the data say about their initial level is little, and a model that sees only these cells has to rely on its prior.

### The Hierarchical Model

The observation layer is a Beta regression, as in Part 2.[^3] The state of health $y_{ij}$ of cell $j$ at its cycle $c_{ij}$ follows a Beta distribution with mean $\mu_{ij}$ and precision $\phi$,

$$
y_{ij} \sim \mathrm{Beta}\big(\mu_{ij}\phi,\ (1-\mu_{ij})\phi\big),
$$

and the mean is linked to the linear predictor by the inverse logit,

$$
\mu_{ij} = \mathrm{logit}^{-1}(\eta_{ij}).
$$

The linear predictor on the logit scale combines the ageing of the cell with the diagnostics $\mathbf{x}_{ij}$,

$$
\eta_{ij} = \alpha_j - A_k\, g_j(c_{ij}) + \mathbf{x}_{ij}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta},
$$

where ageing is a saturating exponential of the cycle,

$$
g_j(c) = 1 - e^{-\lambda_j c}.
$$

Here $\alpha_j$ is the initial level of cell $j$, $\lambda_j$ its rate, $A_k$ the amplitude of the chemistry $k$ to which it belongs, and the cycle is counted in thousands. The hierarchy ties the cell parameters to the chemistry. Each chemistry has an initial level $a_k$, a log rate $\ell_k$ and an amplitude $A_k$, drawn from distributions that are shared by the fleet, and a cell departs from its chemistry by an offset,

$$
\alpha_j = a_k + \sigma_{a,k}\, z_{a,j},
$$

$$
\log\lambda_j = \ell_k + \sigma_{\ell,k}\, z_{\ell,j},
$$

where the offsets $z_{a,j}$ and $z_{\ell,j}$ have a standard normal distribution.

The unit-normal offsets $z$ are sampled and scaled afterwards, which is known as a non-centred parameterisation. It matters when the spread between cells is small, because a model that samples $\alpha_j$ directly then has a funnel-shaped posterior that the sampler traverses poorly and reports as divergences.[^4]

The code defines one function for the three strategies, so that they differ in nothing else. For complete pooling the three parameters are single numbers, for no pooling each cell has its own with an independent prior, and for partial pooling they follow the hierarchy above. The hidden cell below builds the three models and fits them, as the section on sampling describes.

Show the model and its fits

``` python
models = {
    pooling_level: hier.hierarchical_model(train, scaler, FEATURES, pooling_level) for pooling_level in hier.POOLING
}
print({pooling_level: len(model.free_RVs) for pooling_level, model in models.items()})
fits = {
    pooling_level: hier.sample(
        models[pooling_level], CACHE / f"train-{pooling_level}.nc", seed=2026 + index, log_likelihood=True, **MAIN
    )
    for index, pooling_level in enumerate(hier.POOLING)
}
```

### Priors and Prior Checks

A prior states what the model believes before it sees any data, and the quickest way to understand one is to look at it. [Figure 3](#fig-priors) draws the prior of each quantity that the model learns. The priors are weakly informative, which means that they rule out values that no battery could show and leave the rest to the data.[^5] The initial level has a normal prior centred on 2 with a standard deviation of 1 at the fleet level, which puts the state of health near 97% for a cell with no ageing term and no diagnostic effect. The log rate is centred on $\log 5$ per thousand cycles with a standard deviation of 0.5, so the saturating term of an ageing cell reaches half of its amplitude after about 140 cycles. The amplitude has a half-normal prior, which allows a small ageing term or a large one but not a negative one. The effect of each standardised diagnostic has a normal prior with a standard deviation of 0.2, so that a feature has to earn a large coefficient, and the standard deviations between cells and between chemistries have half-normal priors, as is usual for scale parameters. The precision $\phi$ of the Beta likelihood has a log-normal prior centred on 100, which corresponds to noise of about 5 points of state of health at mid-life. [Table 1](#tbl-priors) lists them all.

Show the code

``` python
display(tables.themed_gt(priors.hierarchical()))
```

| Parameter | Prior | Role |
|----|----|----|
| Fleet level of α | Normal(2, 1) | Mean initial level across chemistries |
| Spread of α between chemistries | HalfNormal(1) | How far chemistries differ in initial level |
| Fleet level of ln λ | Normal(ln 5, 0.5²) | Mean log rate across chemistries |
| Spread of ln λ between chemistries | HalfNormal(0.5) | How far chemistries differ in rate |
| Amplitude scale | HalfNormal(1) | Scale of the chemistry amplitudes |
| Amplitude A of a chemistry | HalfNormal(scale) | Size of the decay of a chemistry |
| Spread of α, ln λ between cells | HalfNormal(0.5) | How far a cell departs from its chemistry |
| Effects β | Normal(0, 0.2²) | Effect of each standardised diagnostic |
| Precision φ | LogNormal(ln 100, 1) | Noise of the Beta likelihood |

Table 1: Priors of the hierarchical Beta regression. The fleet level and the spreads are shared, and each cell draws its parameters from its chemistry through the cell spreads.

Show the draws of the prior

``` python
with models["partial"]:
    prior = pm.sample_prior_predictive(draws=500, random_seed=1)
    prior_many = pm.sample_prior_predictive(draws=3000, random_seed=2)
prior_soh = prior.prior_predictive["y"].to_numpy().ravel() * hier.CEILING * 100
drawn = np.random.default_rng(1).choice(prior_soh, size=min(20000, prior_soh.size), replace=False)
update = hier.prior_posterior(prior_many, fits["partial"])
QUANTITIES = list(hier.PRIOR_LEVELS.values()) + ["Precision (log10)"]
```

Figure 3: Prior densities of the initial level, the log rate and the amplitude of a chemistry, and of the precision of the Beta likelihood on a logarithmic scale, each drawn before the model sees any data.

The four priors are broad on purpose. The initial level and the log rate cover every ageing curve that a lithium-ion cell could plausibly follow, the amplitude allows any size of ageing term, and the precision prior expects the noise of a fair sensor, not of a cell that one diagnostic describes almost exactly. A prior that is broad in this way commits the model to very little, and the posterior shows how much the data then changed it. What the four priors imply together for the state of health can be checked before any data are used, by drawing parameters from the priors and simulating the cells that they describe. [Figure 4](#fig-prior) compares the state of health of that prior predictive distribution with the observed values of the training cells.

Show the code of the figure

``` python
show(lambda: hierarchy.prior(train["soh"].to_numpy(), drawn))
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 4: Observed state of health of the training cells in blue and the prior predictive distribution of the model in slate, as densities against the state of health in percent.

The prior has its 5th, 50th and 95th percentiles at 23.6%, 91.1% and 109.1%, against 50.8%, 81.9% and 97.7% in the data. It is wider than the data at both ends and its median lies nine points above the observed one, and some of its mass exceeds 100%, which the data also do in 1.7% of the cycles. A weak prior should rule out the impossible and leave the rest to the data, and this one does.

### Posterior Sampling

The posteriors are sampled with the No-U-Turn sampler.[^6] Every fit runs four chains of 500 draws after 750 tuning draws, with a target acceptance rate of 0.90. This post fits the three models of the training cells and two refits for the check of the prior, and the next post refits the models for the test of new cells. Sampling is the slow part, with each hierarchical fit taking several minutes on a laptop, so the notebook stores each fit in a `cache` folder and reads it back on a repeat run.

#### Convergence of the Chains

None of the three fits on the training cells has a divergent transition. The worst $\hat{R}$, the disagreement between chains, is 1.000 for partial pooling, 1.010 for complete pooling and 1.020 for no pooling, against a common guide of 1.01,[^7] and the smallest bulk effective sample sizes are 820, 1,008 and 392, so the no-pooling model is the least well behaved. The two refits of the check of the prior, which is described below, have a worst $\hat{R}$ of 1.01 and a smallest bulk effective sample size of 769. Two divergent transitions occur in the 4,000 draws of the refit under the wide prior, and its estimates agree with those of the other fits, as the check of the prior shows.

Show the checks of the sampler

``` python
for pooling_level, idata in fits.items():
    report = hier.convergence(idata)
    print(
        f"{pooling_level}: {idata.posterior.sizes['chain']} chains of {idata.posterior.sizes['draw']} draws, {report['divergences']} divergences, max R-hat {report['r_hat']:.3f}, min ESS bulk {report['ess_bulk']:.0f}, min ESS tail {report['ess_tail']:.0f}"
    )
```

### From Prior to Posterior

The data turn each prior into a posterior, and the distance between the two says how much the data taught the model. [Figure 5](#fig-update) draws the log rate of each chemistry and the precision, each against its prior. Where a posterior is narrow and far from the prior, the data decided the answer, and where it stays close to the prior, the prior did. The first quantity decides how quickly the ageing term of a chemistry saturates, and the second decides how closely the model believes that its predictions follow the observations, so together they show where the data were informative and where they were not.

Show the code of the figure

``` python
for quantity in ("Log rate (per 1,000 cycles)", "Precision (log10)"):
    show(lambda quantity=quantity: hierarchy.priors(update, quantity, COLOURS))
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

\(a\) Log rate (per 1,000 cycles)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

\(b\) Precision (log10)

Figure 5: Prior and posterior of the log rate of each chemistry, and of the precision on a logarithmic scale. The slate curve is the prior, blue is CS2 and the posterior of the precision, and orange is CX2.

The log rate of the two chemistries moved well away from the prior, which is centred on $\log 5 = 1.61$. The posterior mean is $-0.31$ for CS2 and 0.73 for CX2, so the data separated the chemistries and placed both well below the prior. The posterior of CS2 is the broader of the two, with a 90% interval from $-0.78$ to 0.30 against 0.44 to 1.05 for CX2, because fewer cells inform it and they differ from one another. The precision moved furthest. Its posterior mean is 1,810 against a prior centred on 100, and the prior puts only 0.2% of its mass above that value, so the figure shows it on a logarithmic scale, where the posterior is a narrow spike at 3.26 far to the right of a prior centred on 2. The data are therefore far more precise than the prior expected, because one diagnostic nearly determines the state of health. This is the one prior of the model that the data contradict, and a later section tests whether it matters.

### Posterior of the Chemistries

The chemistry level of the hierarchical model is where the model says something that a single curve cannot. [Figure 6](#fig-chemistry) shows the posterior of the three parameters for each chemistry, one parameter in each panel. They differ in all three. The initial level is 1.19 for CS2 (90% interval 1.08 to 1.32) and 1.98 for CX2 (1.72 to 2.22) on the logit scale. The amplitude of the saturating term is 2.76 for CS2 (2.33 to 3.29) and 1.03 for CX2 (1.01 to 1.06). The log rate is $-0.31$ for CS2 (from $-0.78$ to 0.30) and 0.73 for CX2 (from 0.44 to 1.05), and the posterior probability that the rate of CX2 exceeds that of CS2 is 0.992.

``` python
    show(lambda quantity=quantity: hierarchy.chemistry(draws, COLOURS, quantity))
```

\(a\) Initial level (logit)

Figure 6: Posterior density of the three chemistry parameters, for CS2 in blue and CX2 in orange. The further apart the curves, the more surely the chemistries differ.

Read together, the three describe the curves of [Figure 2](#fig-curves). The CX2 term is small and saturates early, with a half-time of about 330 cycles, so the long, slow decline of those cells is carried by the diagnostics. The CS2 term is large and slow, with a half-time of about 950 cycles, so those cells keep losing capacity over their whole life. The difference between the chemistries is larger than the difference between cells within one. The standard deviation between cells of the log rate is 0.52 in CS2 and 0.47 in CX2, against a gap of 1.04 between the chemistries, and for the initial level it is 0.14 and 0.34, against a gap of 0.79. Only two chemistries inform these standard deviations, so they are set partly by their priors and are not interpreted further.

Of the four diagnostics, only the area under the discharge voltage has an effect that differs from zero beyond doubt, at 0.362 with a posterior standard deviation of 0.016, and the other three lie within two standard deviations of zero. The precision $\phi$ is about 1,800, which corresponds to a noise standard deviation of about one point of state of health. That is far in the upper tail of its prior, which puts 0.2% of its mass above 1,800, and it says that one diagnostic nearly determines the state of health, which has consequences for the tests that follow.

#### Cell Shrinkage

The hierarchy also changes what is said about a single cell. [Figure 7](#fig-shrinkage) sets the estimate of each training cell without pooling, hollow, beside the estimate with partial pooling, filled, with the posterior mean of the chemistry as a dashed line.

Show the code of the figure

``` python
chemistry_of = train.drop_duplicates("cell").set_index("cell")["CellType"]
cells = [cell for chemistry in CHEMISTRIES for cell in chemistry_of[chemistry_of == chemistry].index]
estimates, means = hier.shrinkage_frames(fits["none"], fits["partial"], chemistry_of, cells)
for parameter in ("Initial level (logit)", "Log rate (per 1,000 cycles)"):
    show(lambda parameter=parameter: hierarchy.shrinkage(estimates, means, COLOURS, cells, parameter))
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

\(a\) Initial level (logit)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

\(b\) Log rate (per 1,000 cycles)

Figure 7: Estimates of a parameter of each training cell without pooling (hollow) and with partial pooling (filled), with the posterior mean of each chemistry as a dashed line.

The largest change is for the cell with the least complete record. The initial level of CX2_16, whose record begins at cycle 463, moves from 3.54 without pooling to 1.96 with it, close to the 1.98 of its chemistry, and CX2_33, which begins at cycle 187, moves from 2.09 to 1.74. The other cells change by 0.12 or less. Without pooling, the initial level of a cell with no early record is set by the prior and by observations far from cycle zero, and the hierarchy replaces that with what its chemistry shows.

The log rate changes more widely, by up to 0.94 in CS2_35 and 0.92 in CS2_33, although those cells have complete records. On a curve that has not yet saturated, the rate and the amplitude trade off against each other, so a cell’s rate is poorly determined on its own, and the shared amplitude of its chemistry fixes part of that trade. This reading is consistent with the figure but was not tested separately. Averaged over the training cells, an estimate differs by 0.24 logit units for the initial level and by 0.40 for the log rate between the two strategies.

### Sensitivity to the Prior

The posterior of the precision lies far from its prior, and a prior that is far from the data can decide the answer when the data are few. With 1,456 observations that is unlikely, but the question can be answered by computation and the limits of the first version of this study left it open. The model is therefore refitted with a narrow prior for the precision, a log-normal distribution centred on 100 whose logarithm has a standard deviation of 0.3, and with a wide prior centred on 1,000 whose logarithm has a standard deviation of 1.5, against the default of 1.0 centred on 100. [Figure 8](#fig-sensitivity) draws the posterior of the log rate of each chemistry under the three priors, with the default fit as the heavier line.

Show the refits under other priors

``` python
sensitivity_fits = {}
for index, (setting, phi_prior) in enumerate(PHI_PRIORS.items()):
    if setting.startswith("Default"):
        sensitivity_fits[setting] = fits["partial"]  # the fit of the post, not a second copy of it
        continue
    model = hier.hierarchical_model(train, scaler, FEATURES, "partial", phi_prior=phi_prior)
    sensitivity_fits[setting] = hier.sample(
        model, CACHE / f"prior-phi-{setting.split(',')[0].lower()}.nc", seed=4000 + index, **REFIT
    )
sensitivity = hier.prior_sensitivity(sensitivity_fits)
sensitivity_draws = hier.sensitivity_draws(sensitivity_fits)
for setting, idata in sensitivity_fits.items():
    report = hier.convergence(idata)
    print(
        f"{setting}: {report['divergences']} divergences, max R-hat {report['r_hat']:.3f}, min ESS bulk {report['ess_bulk']:.0f}"
    )
```

Show the code of the figure

``` python
for chemistry in CHEMISTRIES:
    show(lambda chemistry=chemistry: hierarchy.sensitivity(sensitivity_draws, chemistry))
```

Figure 8: Posterior density of the log rate of each chemistry under a narrow, a default and a wide prior for the precision of the Beta likelihood.

The three curves of each chemistry lie almost on top of one another. The posterior mean of the log rate of CS2 is $-0.36$, $-0.32$ and $-0.33$ under the narrow, the default and the wide prior, and that of CX2 is 0.73, 0.73 and 0.74. The probability that the rate of CX2 exceeds that of CS2 is 0.996, 0.992 and 0.990. The initial level and the amplitude of each chemistry agree to within 0.02 across the three priors. The posterior mean of the precision is 1,739, 1,810 and 1,820, which says that the data move the precision from a prior centred on 100 to about 1,800 even when the prior is tight. The conclusions about the chemistries therefore do not depend on the prior of the precision, and the tight prior of the default model does not decide them. The same parameter sets the width of every predictive interval, which the next post checks on the scores.

### Fit on Training Cells

Before the model is tested on cells that it has not seen, it is checked on the cells that it has. Leave-one-out cross-validation scores a model by the log density that it gives to an observation when that observation is left out of the fit, and the average of these scores is the expected log predictive density.[^8] Pareto-smoothed importance sampling approximates the scores from a single fit, and the difference between two models comes with a standard error. The log density is a proper scoring rule, so the model with the larger value is the one whose predictive distribution lies closer to the process that generated the data. Its scale is that of the Beta density of the state of health as a fraction, so only differences between models have a meaning. [Figure 9](#fig-loo) shows, for each of the 11 training cells, how much partial pooling and complete pooling gain over no pooling, and the bars of one model add up to its difference in expected log predictive density. Partial pooling is behind no pooling by 124.6 (standard error 14.5), which is 8.6 standard errors, and complete pooling is behind by 2,242 (standard error 76). Partial pooling is behind in 10 of the 11 cells and its largest loss is 31.3 for CX2_16, while complete pooling is behind in every cell. The effective number of parameters is 63.6 for no pooling, 45.9 for partial pooling and 10.5 for complete pooling. One observation of the no-pooling model and one of the partial-pooling model have a Pareto $k$ above 0.7, so those two totals are a little less certain than the standard errors say.

Show the leave-one-out scores

``` python
labels = {"none": "No pooling", "complete": "Complete pooling", "partial": "Partial pooling"}
named = {labels[pooling_level]: fits[pooling_level] for pooling_level in hier.POOLING}
comparison = az.compare(named, ic="loo")
print(comparison[["elpd_loo", "p_loo", "elpd_diff", "dse"]].round(1).to_string())
by_cell = hier.loo_by_cell(named, train["cell"].to_numpy())
wide = by_cell.pivot(index="cell", columns="method", values="elpd")
gain = wide.sub(wide["No pooling"], axis=0)
print("cells where partial pooling beats no pooling:", int((gain["Partial pooling"] > 0).sum()), "of", len(gain))
print("largest loss of partial pooling:", gain["Partial pooling"].idxmin(), round(gain["Partial pooling"].min(), 1))
print("cells where complete pooling beats no pooling:", int((gain["Complete pooling"] > 0).sum()))
print("observations with Pareto k above 0.7:", by_cell.groupby("method")["bad"].sum().to_dict())
```

``` python
    show(lambda method=method: hierarchy.loo(by_cell, COLOURS, CHEMISTRY_OF, method, "No pooling"))
```

Figure 9: Gain in expected log density of partial pooling and of complete pooling over no pooling, for each cell, from leave-one-out cross-validation. Bars to the left of zero are cells that the model predicts worse.

Cell-specific parameters matter a great deal for cells that are in the data, and the likelihood is so sharp that an offset of two or three points of state of health is worth many units of log density, which is why every cell loses under complete pooling. The same parameters are not available for a new cell, so this ranking does not carry over to one. Leave-one-out here leaves out single cycles, and the neighbouring cycles of the same cell still fix its curve, so it measures how well a model interpolates within cells it has seen and not how well it predicts a cell that it has not. The test of the next post leaves out whole cells and answers that question; a leave-one-cell-out version of this figure would need one refit for each of the 11 cells and each model.

### Limits of the Study

The prior of the precision $\phi$ is tight and the posterior lies far in its upper tail, and the refits above show that the conclusions about the chemistries do not depend on it. Two chemistries are few, because the spread between chemistries is estimated from two groups, so the chemistry-level standard deviations are set partly by their priors and are not interpreted here. The curve is simple, since a saturating exponential with a linear effect of the diagnostics has no knee, which the end of life of these cells shows, and every eighth cycle is used, which shortens the run and discards little, although the observations that remain are still correlated. The residuals are treated as independent, and the next post shows what that costs when the model predicts a cell that it has not seen. The leave-one-out scores of the last section leave out single cycles, so they measure interpolation within the cells of the data and not prediction of a new cell.

### Summary of Findings

A hierarchical model with cells in chemistries separates what belongs to a chemistry from what belongs to a cell. The two chemistries differ in all three curve parameters, with a probability of 0.992 that CX2 has the higher rate, and the conclusion does not change under a narrower or a wider prior for the precision. Partial pooling also steadies the cell whose early life is missing, CX2_16, whose initial level falls from 3.54 to 1.96.

The fit to the cells that the model has seen favours cell-specific parameters, as it should. In leave-one-out cross-validation partial pooling is behind no pooling in 10 of the 11 cells, because the cells in the data fix their own curves, and complete pooling is behind in every cell. That ranking says how well a model interpolates within cells that it has seen and not how it predicts a new one. [The second post of Part 3](../../../../../pages/blog/posts/2026/11/2026-11-28-hierarchical-bayesian-retirement.llms.md) leaves out whole cells, tests the three strategies as predictors of a new cell, and applies the cost-loss rule of an operator to their probabilities.

### Reproducible Results

The notebook is in the [bayesian-modelling](https://github.com/sambaiga/bayesian-modelling) repository and runs from the first cell to the last in the `uv` environment of the repository, with PyMC 5.25, ArviZ 0.22 and lets-plot 4.11, and downloads the feature file when it first runs. The model, the sampling and the figures are functions of the `bayes` package, which has unit tests, and the cells of the notebook only call them. The sampling settings are in the first cell, and setting the environment variable `HIER_FAST=1` runs the whole notebook with a few draws in a minute or two, to check that it works before the full run. The fits are stored in `cache/`, so a repeat of the full run reads them back.
